# Internal Triggers

Internal triggers are experiences that arise within you, like thoughts, emotions, body sensations, or memories, that increase the urge to drink.

Common examples include:

-   Stress, anger, loneliness, shame
-   Overconfidence (“I can handle just one”)
-   Physical discomfort (fatigue, tension)
-   Mental replay of past drinking relief

Internal triggers are especially important because they can occur anytime, anywhere, even in safe environments.

A key skill in recovery is learning to observe inner experiences without automatically acting on them. Urges usually rise and fall like waves. When you label what is happening ("this is anxiety," "this is craving," "this is an old thought"), you create space between feeling and behavior.

In many recovery approaches that focus on thoughts and behaviors, internal triggers are treated as early warning signals rather than commands. The more quickly you notice and name an internal cue, the more options you have to choose a response that protects sobriety.

![](https://github.com/jjcurtin/aud_support/blob/main/modules/images/spark.jpg?raw=true){fig-align="center"}

## Noticing Practice

Complete this practice exercise whenever you notice urges or strong emotions today,

| What I noticed inside me | Intensity (0-10) | What I did instead of drinking | Result after 20 minutes |
|------------------|------------------|------------------|------------------|
|  |  |  |  |
|  |  |  |  |
|  |  |  |  |

*Tip: Even small responses (pause, step away, breathe, distract) count as success if they helped lower your intensity.*

::: callout
## Reflection

Which internal trigger shows up most often for me?

What helps lower it, even slightly?

What early signs can I watch for next time?
:::

**Remember you don’t have to eliminate internal triggers. You can learn to recognize them early and respond intentionally instead of automatically.**
